header: House prep recipes for clarification and washes (after 20261018020000).
Stage 4E of the bottle catalog plan:
* 16 shared catalog preps that had no recipe get one, each from the pages
it cites (one item_sources row per recipe, yield and keep fact; two
sites for the staples): tomato water and clarified tomato water,
clarified lime, lemon, grapefruit, orange, apple, pineapple, watermelon,
guava, coconut and citrus juice (Dave Arnold's agar methods), a milk
wash, clarified and California milk punch, and an olive oil washed
* Clarified guava and coconut apply Arnold's general agar dose to juices
he never tested: they say "Starting point: test a batch first."
* The milk preps say they contain milk. One new plain ingredient:
Cocktail batch (the base a milk wash is poured from).
* An independent second check of every fact in this stage (64) against
the cited pages found 4 wrong, all keeps that took the long end of a
range (clarified citrus, milk wash, both milk punches). All four are

ingredients.name: Cocktail batch
ingredients.description: Any drink mixed ahead in bulk before dilution or service. Used as the base for milk washes and punches.

preps.name: Clarified apple juice
preps.description: Fresh apple juice cleared with a weak agar gel, a third of it boiled with the agar and the rest whisked in cold. Clear, crisp apple for highballs, spritzes and carbonated drinks.

steps.body: Whisk the agar into the smaller portion of cold juice, bring it to the boil while stirring, then simmer a couple of minutes so the agar hydrates.
Whisking hard, pour the rest of the cold juice into the boiling mix in a thin stream. Don't let it fall below 35 °C before it's all in or it sets in lumps.
Set the bowl over an ice bath until it firms to a soft, loose gel.
Break the gel into curds with a whisk, tip into a cheesecloth-lined sieve and let it drain. Stir the curds or twist the cloth gently; pressing hard pushes agar through.
Pass through a coffee filter if any agar specks got through, then bottle and chill.

sources.note: Arnold: juice that can take some heat has a third boiled with the agar (0.2% of the total) and two thirds whisked in cold; his orange batch is 250 g + 500 g + 1.5 g. Doubled to 500 g + 1000 g + 3 g.
Team Lyan's quick gel: agar at 0.02% of the liquid weight, a tenth of Arnold's figure and most likely a misprint. We use Arnold's measured 0.2% (2 g per kilo).

preps.name: Clarified citrus
preps.description: Lime (or lemon) juice made crystal clear with a weak agar gel, so it carbonates well and looks clean in clear drinks. Make it the day you use it.

recipe.note: freshly squeezed, room temperature; lemon works the same way

steps.body: Whisk the agar into the water, bring it to the boil and let it simmer a couple of minutes, whisking, until clear.
Off the heat, whisk the room temperature juice into the hot agar water. The mix should land near 39 °C; never boil the juice.
Leave it in the fridge or over ice until it sets to a soft gel.
Break the gel up gently with a whisk and pour it into a sieve lined with three layers of cheesecloth.
Massage the cloth gently to let the clear juice out. Squeezing hard pushes agar through; run it through a coffee filter if any bits get past.

sources.note: Dave Arnold's quick agar clarification for heat-sensitive lime juice: 375 g juice, 1 g agar boiled in 125 g water, juice tempered in. His orange juice test returned about 69% (516.8 g from 750 g); our yield applies that.
Arnold: clarified lime must be used the day it is made, not even the next morning; recorded as 12 hours.
The original method: agar at 0.2% of the juice weight, set, broken and drained through cheesecloth; 516.8 g clear juice back from 750 g orange juice.

preps.name: Clarified coconut
preps.description: Coconut water set with a weak agar gel and drained crystal clear, for clear tropical drinks and highballs. Starting point: test a batch first.

steps.body: Whisk the agar into the water, bring it to the boil and let it simmer a couple of minutes, whisking, until clear.
Off the heat, whisk the room temperature juice into the hot agar water. The mix should land near 39 °C; never boil the juice.
Leave it in the fridge or over ice until it sets to a soft gel.
Break the gel up gently with a whisk and pour it into a sieve lined with three layers of cheesecloth.
Massage the cloth gently to let the clear juice out. Squeezing hard pushes agar through; run it through a coffee filter if any bits get past.

sources.note: Dave Arnold's quick agar ratio (2 g agar per kg of juice 'or whatever'), in his heat-sensitive form: 375 g liquid, 1 g agar boiled in 125 g water. He did not test coconut water, so this is untested arithmetic.
The 0.2% agar method in full, and hydrating agar in water for liquids that can't be boiled.

preps.name: Clarified grapefruit juice
preps.description: Fresh grapefruit juice cleared with a weak agar gel. Clarifying leaves it clean and bright, with less bitterness, and it carbonates far better than cloudy juice: think clear Palomas and highballs.

steps.body: Let the juice come to room temperature (about 25 °C). Whisk the agar into the water and bring it to the boil, whisking, then simmer a couple of minutes so it hydrates.
Off the heat, pour the juice into the hot agar water in a thin stream, whisking hard. Never boil the juice, and don't let the mix fall below 35 °C before it's all in or it sets in lumps.
Set the bowl over an ice bath until it firms to a soft, loose gel.
Break the gel into curds with a whisk, tip into a cheesecloth-lined sieve and let it drain. Stir the curds or twist the cloth gently; pressing hard pushes agar through.
Pass through a coffee filter if any agar specks got through, then bottle and chill.

sources.note: Arnold's quick agar clarification: agar at 0.2% of the total weight; heat-sensitive juice stays unboiled, 4 parts room-temperature juice to 1 part water that the agar is boiled in. Scaled to 800 g juice, 200 g water, 2 g agar.
Team Lyan's quick gel: agar at 0.02% of the liquid weight, a tenth of Arnold's figure and most likely a misprint. We use Arnold's measured 0.2% (2 g per kilo).
Arnold on clarified grapefruit: tastes clean and bright and loses some bitterness; he also clarifies it with gelatin. We treat it as fresh citrus and keep it unboiled.

recipe.note: room temperature, sieved first if pulpy

preps.description: Fresh lemon juice cleared with a weak agar gel, which traps the haze so the juice drains out clear. For clear sours, carbonated drinks and stirred drinks that want lemon. Made like Arnold's lime, unboiled.

preps.name: Clarified lime juice
preps.description: Fresh lime juice cleared with a weak agar gel, which traps the haze so the juice drains out water-clear. For clear sours, carbonated drinks and stirred drinks that want lime; use it the day it's made.

steps.body: Let the juice come to room temperature (about 25 °C). Whisk the agar into the water and bring it to the boil, whisking, then simmer a couple of minutes so it hydrates.
Off the heat, pour the juice into the hot agar water in a thin stream, whisking hard. Never boil the juice, and don't let the mix fall below 35 °C before it's all in or it sets in lumps.
Set the bowl over an ice bath until it firms to a soft, loose gel.
Break the gel into curds with a whisk, tip into a cheesecloth-lined sieve and let it drain. Stir the curds or twist the cloth gently; pressing hard pushes agar through.
Pass through a coffee filter if any agar specks got through. Chill and use the same day.

sources.note: Arnold's quick agar clarification: agar at 0.2% of the total weight; heat-sensitive juice stays unboiled, 4 parts room-temperature juice to 1 part water that the agar is boiled in. Scaled to 800 g juice, 200 g water, 2 g agar.
Team Lyan's quick gel: agar at 0.02% of the liquid weight, a tenth of Arnold's figure and most likely a misprint. We use Arnold's measured 0.2% (2 g per kilo).
Arnold: clarified lime keeps no better than fresh lime and must be used the day it's made. We record that as 12 hours.

preps.name: Clarified milk punch
preps.description: A batched gin, lemon and Earl Grey punch poured into milk so the curds filter it clear, silky and shelf stable. Bottle it and pour over ice. Contains milk: drinks made with it carry milk as an allergen.

recipe.note: brewed strong: 2 heaped tsp leaves per 240 ml hot water, cooled

steps.body: Brew the Earl Grey strong, strain out the leaves and let it cool.
Mix the gin, lemon, syrup and tea. If there is time, let the batch sit a few hours.
Pour about a third of the batch into the cold milk (never the milk into the batch) and stir once. When it breaks, add the rest gently without stirring.
Cover and rest in the fridge at least 24 hours; 48 is better.
Strain a scoop at a time through a coffee filter or a sieve lined with double cheesecloth. Pour the first cloudy run back through. Never press the curds.
Bottle and keep cold. Contains milk.

sources.note: Mia Glanz's Earl Grey milk punch, batched x10: 20 oz gin, 7.5 oz lemon, 5 oz simple syrup, 20 oz Earl Grey tea (600 / 225 / 150 / 600 ml at 30 ml per oz), with milk at 4 parts batch to 1 (about 395 ml); rest 24 to 48 h.

Campari Academy: milk is batch volume x 0.25 (the same 4:1), and their test sour ran 2 vodka : 0.75 lemon : 0.75 simple syrup with 20% milk, no tea. Sweeter than Glanz's; we use Glanz's spec and Campari's third-first pouring.
After a week or two the solids drop out and it needs refiltering; we take the short end, a week.

preps.name: Clarified orange juice
preps.description: Orange juice cleared with a weak agar gel: a third of the juice is boiled with the agar, the rest whisked in cold. Arnold's own worked example; clear orange for stirred and carbonated drinks.

steps.body: Whisk the agar into the smaller portion of cold juice, bring it to the boil while stirring, then simmer a couple of minutes so the agar hydrates.
Whisking hard, pour the rest of the cold juice into the boiling mix in a thin stream. Don't let it fall below 35 °C before it's all in or it sets in lumps.
Set the bowl over an ice bath until it firms to a soft, loose gel.
Break the gel into curds with a whisk, tip into a cheesecloth-lined sieve and let it drain. Stir the curds or twist the cloth gently; pressing hard pushes agar through.
Pass through a coffee filter if any agar specks got through, then bottle and chill.

sources.note: Arnold's worked example as written: 1.5 g agar (0.2%) boiled in 250 g cold orange juice, then 500 g cold juice whisked in.
Arnold got 516.8 g of clear juice from this 750 g batch, from unstrained juice.

preps.description: Fresh pineapple juice cleared with a weak agar gel, a third of it boiled with the agar and the rest whisked in cold. Clear pineapple for stirred tiki riffs and carbonated drinks.

preps.name: Clarified tomato water
preps.description: Tomato purée set with a little gelatine, frozen and thawed slowly through cloth, so only crystal-clear tomato water drips out. The clearest tomato water for stirred drinks and carbonating.

steps.body: Blend the tomatoes smooth. Don't salt them yet: what drips out first is more concentrated.
Bloom the gelatine in a little cold purée, melt it into a small warmed portion, then stir that through the rest.
Pour into a shallow tray, leave it in the fridge a while so the gelatine can work, then freeze it solid.
Set the frozen block in a cloth-lined perforated pan or sieve over a container and let it thaw in the fridge. Don't press it.
Stir all the drips together before bottling: the first ones carry most of the flavour, sugar and acid.

sources.note: Arnold's gelatin freeze-thaw: 5 g gelatin per kilo of product, rested in the fridge, frozen solid, thawed in the fridge over cheesecloth; batch all the drips together. Used as written for 1 kg.
Damini brothers' tomato water: 400 g blitzed tomatoes with 2 g powdered gelatine (0.5%, the same ratio), frozen at least 8 hours and thawed in muslin in the fridge.

preps.name: Clarified watermelon juice
preps.description: Fresh watermelon juice cleared with a weak agar gel into a pale, clear juice in under an hour. For clear coolers, spritzes and carbonated drinks.

steps.body: Let the juice come to room temperature (about 25 °C). Whisk the agar into the water and bring it to the boil, whisking, then simmer a couple of minutes so it hydrates.
Off the heat, pour the juice into the hot agar water in a thin stream, whisking hard. Never boil the juice, and don't let the mix fall below 35 °C before it's all in or it sets in lumps.
Set the bowl over an ice bath until it firms to a soft, loose gel.
Break the gel into curds with a whisk, tip into a cheesecloth-lined sieve and let it drain. Stir the curds or twist the cloth gently; pressing hard pushes agar through.
Pass through a coffee filter if any agar specks got through, then bottle and chill.

sources.note: Arnold's quick agar clarification, unboiled version for delicate juice: 4 parts room-temperature juice to 1 part water the agar is boiled in, agar 0.2% of the total. Scaled to 800 g juice. A reader on the page reports watermelon clear in under an hour.

preps.name: Milk punch
preps.description: Jerry Thomas's bottling milk punch from 1887: brandy, Jamaican rum and arrack steeped with lemon, pineapple, spice and green tea, then broken with hot milk and filtered bright. Serve iced. Contains milk: drinks made with it carry milk as an allergen.

recipe.note: juiced: 4 at the start, 2 more with the milk
dissolved in just enough hot water

steps.body: Put the juice of 4 lemons, the rind of 2, the dissolved sugar, pounded pineapple, spices, brandy, rum, arrack and tea in a large clean jar. Add the boiling water last.
Seal it so nothing evaporates and steep at least 6 hours.
Add the hot milk and the juice of 2 more lemons and mix.
Filter through a jelly bag or coffee filter until it runs bright. Do not press.
Bottle tightly and keep cold; serve over ice. For same-day use the source says filtering can be skipped. Contains milk.

sources.note: Jerry Thomas, Bar-Tender's Guide (1887), p. 86, California Milk Punch for bottling (public domain). Converted: pint 480 ml, quart 960 ml, gill 120 ml, cup 240 ml, half a pound of sugar about 225 g.
After a week or two the solids drop out and it needs refiltering; we take the short end, a week.

preps.name: Milk wash
preps.description: The base ratio for milk washing: a sour or tannic batch poured into a quarter of its volume of milk, rested and filtered through the curds until clear and silky. Contains milk: drinks made with it carry milk as an allergen.

recipe.note: must taste sour or tannic: citrus, tea, coffee or wine
only if the batch has no acid or tannin, to taste

steps.body: Make sure the batch tastes sour or tannic. If not, add some acid.
Pour about a third of the batch into the milk (never the milk into the batch) and stir. Stop when it breaks.
Add the rest gently without stirring and leave it at least 15 minutes, up to a few hours.
Strain through a coffee filter or nut-milk bag. Pour the first cloudy run back through once the curds form a mat. Never press.
Bottle and chill. Contains milk.

sources.note: Campari Academy: milk volume is batch volume x 0.25; add a third of the batch to the milk first, rest 15 minutes to a few hours. Their lab test used 20% milk. Scaled to a 1 litre batch.
Mia Glanz uses 4 parts cocktail to 1 part milk, the same as Campari's; she notes many bartenders use 6:1.
After a week or two the solids drop out and it needs refiltering; we take the short end, a week.

preps.name: Olive oil washed vodka
preps.description: Vodka rested with extra virgin olive oil, then frozen so the oil sets and lifts off, leaving a rounder, peppery, grassy spirit for Martinis.

steps.body: Combine the vodka and olive oil in a freezer-safe container.
Leave it at room temperature for 5 days.
Freeze until the oil sets into a solid layer.
Break through the oil, lift it off and strain the vodka through cheesecloth or a coffee filter.
Bottle and keep in the fridge.

sources.note: Mark Bystrom (Forequarter, Madison): 250 ml vodka to 45 ml extra virgin olive oil, 5 days at room temperature, then frozen and the oil scraped off. Scaled to a 750 ml bottle (135 ml oil).
Shy Shy's Caesar vodka washes a 750 ml bottle with 3 oz (90 ml) olive oil, freezes, then strains through cheesecloth. Lighter than Forequarter's; we use Forequarter's plain-vodka ratio.
Drinks World's general fat wash runs 1 to 2 oz (30 to 60 ml) fat per 750 ml, far lighter; olive oil washes in bar recipes run heavier, so we use Forequarter's.
General guidance for fat-washed spirits, fridge: about 1 to 2 weeks; we take the shorter. (Shy Shy says indefinitely; we use the cautious figure.)

preps.name: Tomato water
preps.description: The pale, savoury liquid that drips from blended salted tomatoes left to hang in cloth. Brings fresh tomato and umami to Martinis, highballs and Bloody Mary riffs without the pulp.

recipe.note: ripe, quartered, with all juice and seeds

steps.body: Quarter ripe tomatoes, keeping all their juice and seeds, and blend with the salt until smooth.
Pour into a cheesecloth-lined sieve (or a coffee filter) over a clean bowl.
Let it drip in the fridge for several hours or overnight. Don't press, squeeze or stir, or it turns cloudy.
Bottle the clear liquid and keep it cold.

sources.note: Little Sister's tomato water: 2 lb tomatoes blended with a pinch of salt and strained clear through a coffee filter. 2 lb taken as about 900 g.

Ode to Tomatoes: 2 quarts cherry tomatoes salted with 1 tsp kosher salt (herbs optional), pulsed and drained overnight through cheesecloth in the fridge. Salts much harder than Imbibe; we use Imbibe's pinch, and this page's cloth drip.
A week in the fridge, for this same pinch-salted tomato water.
3 to 4 days in the fridge for a herb and salt tomato water salted a little harder than ours; we take 3 days, the shorter keep. Another Imbibe tomato water (Eden's River) says to use it immediately.
